utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. While we are waiting for the witness, may I take this opportunity to ask both parties, in particular the Prosecutor, whether they would be prepared to file a supplementary legal brief on the notion of persecution. This notion was touched upon in the pre-trial brief and reference was made to the brief of argument of the Prosecution in Tadic. Now, I have studied carefully the relevant passages, and I think that we need some more case law, particularly case law, other than The Hague case law of our Tribunal, on the specific point of whether and to what extent an offence, a murder, may be charged as such and also as a persecution. It is a tricky point, and we would like to have some case law on this particular matter or some thinking so that we can start reflecting on this particular problem, say, two, three weeks' time; and, of course, any legal brief from the Defence counsel would be most welcome on the same issue, the notion of persecution. In other cases, we have asked both parties to file simultaneously supplementary briefs. I remember in Dokmanovic, we did so. Probably three weeks' time, in three weeks' time, you could probably, if it is enough time for you, you could file a brief on this particular legal issue? It's a legal issue. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, we have now Witness B. I will call upon Mr. Radovic to start his cross-examination. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, according to our proposed order, Mr. Pavkovic would be the first this morning, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was simply sticking to the order suggested yesterday by Mr. Pavkovic himself but, of course, you are most welcome to speak now and cross-examine the witness. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Reflecting upon the forthcoming cross-examination of this witness, it seemed to me that I couldn't put many questions to this witness or, rather, any questions without calling in question the right of the witness to the protection of his identity. So, Mr. President, I would request that we carry out this cross-examination in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, all right. We will go into a closed session. Could you wait for a few seconds? Thank you. We are now in closed session. You may proceed. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony yesterday, you said that on the 15th of April, 1992 you saw Vlatko Kupreskic. Can you please tell us how Vlatko Kupreskic was dressed on that day in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. You probably want me to tell you the colour of the shirt or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think anything. I'm just asking you. So you can't recollect. Can you remember if he was wearing civilian or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajina. Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I shall also ask a few questions that might reveal the identity of the witness, so could we please go into closed session again? I'm sorry, but we have to be very cautious, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we go back into closed session. Yes, we are now in closed session. You may proceed. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number, for at least another 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have to question the witness from our angle as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, of course. No, no, you are entitled --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This is another series of questions, so if you feel it appropriate for us to have a break, maybe this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that my colleagues agree that we should take a break now, so we will take a break of 30 minutes, as usual, and we will start again at 20 past 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had a rest? Can we resume now?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed to questions regarding the 20th of October, and some points need further clarification, in my opinion. I would like to know whether the decision on the roadblock or a barricade, or whatever you want to call it, was taken by the TO to staff in Vitez, or was the decision taken by higher level command, which was then conveyed to the TO to command in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The important thing is that we should not dispute the name for this obstacle, whether it's a barricade, or a roadblock or whatever, so it's fine. Secondly, the decision was taken by the staff in Vitez. Whether it was the staff commander who had the approval of the district staff from Zenica, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because according to a witness statement disclosed to us by the Prosecution, some claim that the order came from Sarajevo, others that it came from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you stick by your statement that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know whether it came from Zenica. I know that there was a staff meeting, that at the beginning of the meeting Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak and Mario Cerkez arrived, that they made an ultimatum with the commander and that was when the commander made the decision that he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who chose the position where the checkpoint was placed, if we call it that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because from the statement of one of the witnesses whose name I will not mention but I will mention it later -- I haven't mentioned the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: My objection doesn't go to the name, it goes to this practice, I think, of asking a question, getting an, "I don't know," and referring to some other witness's statement in order to explain why the question was being asked. It appears to be time-consuming and unnecessary. If the witness says he does not know, then that's the answer, and to read someone else's statement who says something else and has no relationship with this witness seems, to me, to be just an attempt to make a speech, or at least it's wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I'm sure you have noticed, I am not making speeches, I am asking direct questions. I'm asking whether a witness who was a member of the staff knew something that he should have known as a member of the staff, and if he says that he doesn't know, then the credibility of the witness is in question. I didn't oppose when the Prosecutor put partly guiding -- leading questions, so I think it is not proper for him to interfere with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radovic, it is true that you're not making speeches. On the other hand, I think that the Prosecutor is right when he points out that in a way after getting a no -- a negative response from the witness, there's probably no need for you to explain in detail that actually other witnesses have stated in their witness statements -- have stated something different, totally different. I wonder whether you could probably skip that part and move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: May I then tell the witness in advance what somebody else has said about the same fact before he gives me an answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, in a concise way, and without mentioning the name of the relevant witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will strictly abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that. So tell me now, on the basis of what do you know that there were 2.500 HVO troops on the move? Did you count them, is this an estimate of yours? If it is your estimate, tell us the grounds on which it was made.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We couldn't count, and the data reached us from our men who were in the area where the troops were moving. These reports came from Kiseljak, Busovaca, Kaonik, so that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So the people who saw the column moving. So the estimate was made on the basis of the density of the column, the length of the column?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, the people who saw it moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they couldn't count. They could have said a truck load, and roughly you know how many people can fit into a truck. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So, you see, we do agree more or less regarding these technical matters. My next question will be regarding the personnel that manned this checkpoint. Did they receive any assistance from Poculica, Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I must tell you again that I do not know, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please do. I don't mind at all, on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: At the time of this event, I was in the school where the headquarters were at the time, and the decision was taken in the evening, on the 19th, late in the evening of the 19th of October, 1992. And I don't know exactly the time, but roughly around midnight a shell hit the school, and it had been fired from the direction of the Mlakici houses. It was a hand-held rocket launcher known as a Zolja, for single use, yes. And the marksman wanted to hit the window, because the window of the office had the lights on, because this was a meeting of all the leading Bosniaks in Vitez. I was in another room. So this strong explosion was heard, and the shell hit the wall above the window, it didn't enter the office. And we turned off the lights, and we, in the school, were immediately alerted. The staff, headed by Sefkija and his immediate associates went to Stari Vitez that night, following a route via the pool, and I stayed in the school. I stayed in the school for five days, surrounded. I didn't go out. We were encircled by HVO troops so that I had no idea as to what was happening in Ahmici or in the town itself. I saw that the war was being waged throughout the territory. However, on the fifth day when I went to town there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 20th of October, the TO staff was -- still had control over the people in the TO staff, the brigade had still not been formed; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I must tell you now that we have a statement by a witness who says that it took a long time for the HVO to clear the road from the obstacles and TO troops. So will you tell us how long it took for them to clear the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: He said he was not in Ahmici at the time of this barricade. I fail to see how he could answer that question and why it would be asked of a witness who says he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But he may know --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the shooting could be heard, and if the witness doesn't know on the basis of other information, he at least knows how long the shooting lasted. Everyone knows what an armed conflict looks like, and we know that fire is exchanged in an armed conflict. And on the basis of that, one can come to a conclusion as to how long the conflict lasted. So I would appeal not to be interrupted. So my question is, judging by the fire --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: But you cannot know by the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you can know how long the shooting lasted?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: If there is a conflict, there is an exchange of fire, so you don't know whether the fire is coming just from one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But tell me for how long you could hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While you were in the school, for how long did the fire last?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I couldn't from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't hear the fire?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: If you look at the map and the distance, and if you take into consideration that we were the target of fire and considering the explosions around us, one couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: How long did those explosions around you in the school last?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mean in the school? You're asking about the school, not in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the school. On that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It was not very clear. I do understand the hesitation of the witness. It was not very clear. So now it's in the school. So could you answer this question? Explosions around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long did they last, and whatever it is you were able to hear?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I said that for four days it went on around the school, but with intervals. It didn't go on all day long. But for four days we were blocked in the school and we couldn't leave it. Actually, on the fifth day we were able to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain the fact there were shots fired for four or five days and that approximately the same period it took the HVO to, using the number of 2.500 troops, as you have estimated, to get to you after that period?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There is a certain number of troops that are moving and a certain number of troops that are stopping them?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by clearing the way, the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: To move the Bosniak troops from the road and free the road for the access for the HVO. So the HVO needed to clear the road. Let me simplify what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It didn't take -- according to me and as far as I know, I don't know, it didn't take more than half an hour, because here we didn't have the Armija troops, or the TO troops or the Bosnian troops, which were numerous. As soon as the HVO troops would start firing, they would fire, they would run away, and that's how they cleared the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I request a closed session for a moment, because I would like to mention the testimony of a witness who was on the roadblock, and who stated quite different facts. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now proceed to certain technical questions, and I will here draw on your training in the JNA, hoping that you will answer very briefly. In the anti-aircraft guns, do you immediately see the rounds behind the bullets?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to me in detail where you can see them, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, they are somewhere behind, in the posterior part, on top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you can see it immediately?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a Browning machine gun. Is it the type of machine gun which we received years ago from the American aid; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what sort of aid they come from, but it's the type which, I think, entered Yugoslavia in the course of this conflict. Well, they arrived in Yugoslavia together with the T-47 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were they used in the anti-aircraft defence units?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, they were on the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But when they were carried by the infantry, were they used as sort of back-up weapons for anti-aircraft combats? You know, I served in my military service many years ago, so that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, these were in the armoured tank units in the infantry. Well, I never served in the infantry, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was part of the infantry in my time.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, maybe there was some in the infantry as well, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were learning to apply infantry tactics at school, did you learn that surprising the enemy is contrary to the customs or rules of war? I am asking you this as an expert regardless of the specific conflict or clash concerned.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There's a question which needs to be clarified here because we shouldn't link this directly with this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you in principle whether the factor of surprise is an essential element for the success of combat action?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The factor of surprise is an extremely important factor in an attack mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So as a rule, this is one of the military skills, to surprise the enemy and to supply the enemy with false information?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, in the case of two warring forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also describe to me how does the war doctrine describe a fight in an urban populated area and when you are trying to penetrate a house in which you assume you will come across an armed enemy?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Even the question is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you train the troops to fight in a populated area when they are fighting on the street from one house to another to gain access into a house in a street in which you are fighting if you anticipate armed resistance from this house? I'm not asking you about this specific event, I'm just talking about the military -- the war doctrine in general.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This is being carried out by specially trained units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that the attacks at individual houses are carried out by specially trained units? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, well-trained units. Here we are talking about the principles of war, of a doctrine that studies the events and the situation in a war where an army is fighting another army and the aim is to come near the house undetected and undisclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What do you do first when you arrive in front of a house? I'll be very specific: Do you first throw in a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, you can throw --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The answer was not recorded on my transcript. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You can throw the hand grenade in or next to the house, depending on your intentions, depending on how you want to enter the house, whether you want to get live prisoners or whether you want to kill everybody inside the house instantaneously. There are all sorts of alternatives which you can apply depending on the specific situation. I never entered a house in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were a member of the military police, you were not a member of special units that would be trained for that specific purpose. Tell me, do you know how many Croats who were able to use guns were in Grabova? Grabova, which is the central part of Ahmici where the Kupreskic house was located?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Grabova?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told that's how they refer to this part of Ahmici where the Kupreskic house is located. The central part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: So I should now recall this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly the number. A dozen?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So let's take 20 as a rounded-off figure.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Roughly 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with you because this term of yours, Grabova, is not specified clearly. It's not specified. I don't know exactly what part of the town you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You know, where the Kupreskic houses were located.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, the Kupreskic houses are linked to the Zume houses and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave Zume aside. Let's just stick to this specific part where the Kupreskic house is located, so let's say around 20.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: But then I would also include the Sime, Vinko Vidovic house too, that part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How would you refer to a tactical unit with this number of troops? Is it a platoon? What is it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: A platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The person that commands a platoon, what would such a person be called?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Where do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: JNA? A platoon would be commanded from a lance corporal to a captain, depending on whether you are in the navy, army, or in the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's stick to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, but I see no connection with the JNA here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Does the commander of a tactical unit of a platoon participate in the planning of an attack to be launched at a larger area, such as the one which was attacked on April 16? May I just add: And at what level is this planning done?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There are several levels; however, these questions of yours are equivocal, ambiguous because you are linking me now to the control and command structure in the JNA and applying it to the specific situation in Vitez. These are quite different conditions, quite different organisations, quite different units. It is a completely different type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The JNA consisted of trained professional officers who had graduated from secondary school, from military academies, whose occupation this was; whereas, in this case, people were selected according to their political suitability, a certain level of education, the territory they belonged to, and various other factors. So it wasn't important at that time whether he was a captain or not. We had people in the army, commanders, who had no advanced training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In principle, the commander of a small tactical group, is he capable of participating and does he indeed participate, according to your experience, in the planning of any strategic operations? Let us call them that.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Strategic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I am distinguishing between tactics and strategy.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I make a distinction too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In an organised army, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will accept that answer. On the basis of your experience -- now you must combine your experience from the JNA and the experience you had on the ground -- does a commander of a small territorial unit have any kind of influence over commanders or troops coming to his territory from another area with a particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of influence? Can he take over the command? Did this happen in practice?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The commander of the smaller unit, in cases such as were prevalent at the time, would submit his reports and make his proposals and address requests and, in the case of the transfer of a unit to a particular area or its transfer or its assignment to the command of another unit, either that unit is placed under the command of that unit that is there, local unit, or, if a senior commander so decides, then there may be different alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. There are various possibilities. You mentioned that on the 20th of October, the person killed, Halid Pezer, was about 18, and the Croat who was captured in Vitez, in Old Vitez, was 16. In this most unfortunate war, did young men participate who could be considered children, that is, under 18 years of age, on any side, on both sides or on all three sides?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: As regards the military organisation and as regards the Bosniak side, young men were not mobilised who had not reached the age for doing their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But were they accepted as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: If they applied as volunteers, they would be interviewed. They had to have the approval of their parents and they were not sent to the front-line, but if they were engaged, because the situation was what it was, they would work in the rear, they would carry food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So they were not messengers?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, maybe. What is a messenger, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It is the messenger who carries a message from the command post to an inferior command post or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, they would not be entrusted with confidential information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But if there were regular reports, every day, daily reports that were not confidential?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: If it was something that was not so very important because their seniors were on the front, then perhaps one could call up a young man and tell him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, during the conflict on the 20th of October, any Croats were killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict on the 16th of April, were any Croats killed, and if so, do you know how many?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the weather was like when you realised that there was a battle going on?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mean on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said at the beginning of my question that I was referring to the 16th.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On the 16th? What do you mean, what the conditions were?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Oh, the weather. It was early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I know that. I'm not asking you what time it was, I'm asking was it raining or was it sunny?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The sun had still not risen and it was not raining.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't a drizzle, was there? Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know it wasn't raining, and whether there was that kind of morning haze, I'm not sure. I couldn't leave the house because it was hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, was there a conflict over Ahmici only or was it a broader conflict?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was an all-out attack of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So not on Ahmici alone?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No. It was an attack on the entire territory of Vitez Municipality or, rather, against the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was the road, the Vitez-Busovaca road, of great importance for the HVO, of strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why? I know why, but I would like us to explain it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Because it links Vitez and Busovaca, which had, two or three months previously, been placed under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 16th of April, were there any major conflicts or clashes? Was there any ethnic cleansing, as we call it now, in Lasva and Dusina in January '93 in the area of Busovaca? Dusina. Dusina and Lasva.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I know of some, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know the details?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Croats were expelled from Dusina and Lasva?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: From Dusina?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't really know where that is and still as -- do I know how many Croats there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 15th of April, Zivko Totic was kidnapped and his escort killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the day before the 16th.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As a security officer, did you notice the unrest among the Croats because of this event, because Zivko Totic, as far as I know, was one of the HVO commanders in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: But I wasn't in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you must have followed the reports regarding the overall relations between the Croats and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "unrest."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: They were hurt, offended that Croats in Zenica should be treated in that way, that an HVO commander should be kidnapped in Zenica and his escorting party killed.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Was there concern among the Croats in Vitez, is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know, as far as I understand. Very well. Have you heard of the ethnic cleansing of the Serb village of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs voluntarily abandon the village of Tolovici, and if you know that they did so voluntarily, tell us why, what prompted them to do that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Within the area of Vitez Municipality, there were not many Serbs. I don't know the exact percentage share, but I think two or three per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But as far as I know, Tolovici was one of the few Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I would say the only one. At first, at the beginning, the Croats and the Bosniaks were waging war together against the Serbs. We were together. And every Serb, in those days, was our common enemy so that those Serbs realised that they had nothing to look forward to in Vitez. They were afraid. So they realised that they had to leave and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did some Serbs from Tolovici go to the Croatian part of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know whether they went and who and which is the Croatian part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The part under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No. You are, in your question, you're referring to a Croatian Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I corrected myself by saying the part of the town that was at the time under HVO control. Have I expressed myself clearly? A part of Vitez in those days was under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was in the summer of 1992. Serbs began abandoning Tolovici in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you said that the Croats even then had control over Vitez.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but will you answer my question? Did some Serbs go to that part of Vitez, the new part of Vitez? Let us be even more precise.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Most of them went to the territory under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And the minority?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know about the minority. I know one who went, but he didn't go to the Croats, he went there because there was an area closer to the Bosniaks, Kruscica. He stayed with a relative there. It's called Ciganluk, this area. It is not a Croatian area, it is more a Bosniak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And after the Serbs left, which side entered Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The Bosniak side. They entered because a third of the village was Bosniak, was inhabited by Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So we come to my last question. You said that you were an officer, a security officer, in the Territorial Defence staff in Vitez, and that 25 days after the beginning of the conflict, you left Vitez, as far as I understood. Will you please explain how you left Vitez? In an armoured personnel carrier of the UNPROFOR, as far as I understood you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How come that, as an intelligence officer, you are leaving Vitez at that point in time? Why did you leave it? Why did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I left for the following reasons: Stari Vitez was small in area. It was surrounded on all sides, and no one could leave Stari Vitez. And, really, there was no need for any officers to stay on. There were other people who could do that job. So on the second or third day, we were listening to the radio, and we learnt, through various other messages as well, of the genocide carried out in Ahmici. I didn't know immediately what had happened to my family. I never imagined or dreamt that the genocide could have been of such scope. But one day I was told that Ahmici had been razed to the ground, the population murdered, and I was informed of the deaths in my own family. I heard in Stari Vitez that -- that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you left for family reasons.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Let me not mention all the names of the people who were killed because you know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: So, of course, I was not capable of concentrating anymore, nor was I able to be of any use.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say for family reasons?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The commander, Sefkija, decided that I should leave Stari Vitez, and the personnel carrier came and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, my questions will be very limited in scope and in number, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Witness B, you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Do you think you can put all your questions before the lunch break, say ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Even less. Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you reached Vitez from the former JNA sometime in August. You also said that you joined the TO a little later. Could you tell us exactly when you joined the Territorial Defence? Because "later" could be a year later or two days later.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think it was on the 12th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The 12th of March, '92? Do you know when the Territorial Defence was established?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When did it come into being, the Territorial Defence? You told us when you joined, but can you tell us when it was established?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was a component of the armed forces of the former SFRY, of the former Yugoslavia, which consisted of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. You know very well that all the municipalities had their own Territorial Defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. But let me ask you another question then. At the level of Vitez, was a municipal defence staff set up? Did you join it and when?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We have to clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you please limit yourself to my question: When did you join the staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you joined the staff immediately?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I placed myself at their disposal, but I didn't immediately get an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Fine. But tell me, who appointed the commanders in the various villages? Had they already been appointed when you joined the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you remember what the communication was like between the commanders, the guards, in the villages and the municipal staff in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were there orders, instructions? You know, there must be a hierarchy, a chain of command, so I'm asking whether there were any orders issued by the municipal staff to the lower level, the commanders of units?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I must repeat, there was no proper military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Let's call it a civilian organisation. But my question was: How did the commanders in the villages communicate with the municipal staff in Vitez? Were there instructions or orders between the two? If you don't know, say that. If you can answer it, please give me a "Yes" or "No" answer.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I do know, but I have to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Explain.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: These regional staffs were not armed military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. I said let us call them civilian staffs.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There were lists of civilians made for the purpose of sending them to the front against the Serbs. On the front-line, they would be issued weapons and they had to leave those weapons when they came back. The communication was established personally. An officer would get in touch with a commander and so on. I don't know what you mean, "communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me be more focused. The commander of the village guards, for instance, how did he communicate with the municipal staff? I am repeating my question. Well, you should know as you were a member of that staff.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The commander of the guards, of the watch duty? There was no watch duty in those days. These watches were set up later. You probably have a wrong impression of those guards. On the 16th of April, there were two elderly men who were awake. That was all. They didn't sleep. Just to watch over the situation just in case something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me just tell you that from the statements of other witnesses given to the investigator of the Prosecution, we were told that there were village guards, which is substantially different from what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: But not at that time. You were asking me about the period of the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No, no. That was my question regarding the date when you joined. I asked you what you were doing after that. I can't ask you what you were doing before that because you were not a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The commander had no contact with the guards, with the village guards, and I see no need for him to have any communication with them because this was done in such a way that one or two people would be appointed to keep awake and to observe the situation over night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I already told you that this differs from what other witnesses have said. One further brief question, Mr. President. You said that Zoran Santic was questioned by some people in Stari Vitez and that you entered the room while he was being questioned. Could you tell us when you entered that room, at what point in the questioning? Was the questioning already ongoing by other persons?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What were the first words you heard when you entered, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They were already talking. They were talking already, and I went in and he was saying we are -- he was saying we are talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was a record being kept at the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to the fact that this statement is in contradiction with what you said yesterday because yesterday you said that you heard a dictation being given during the questioning, and that from the dictation, you heard his name which means that you entered the premise before the questioning started, according to what you said yesterday, which means that you were there from the beginning of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain why it is not correct, if I may ask you? You just said that what the Defence counsel said was not correct. What is your recollection? When did you enter the room where Zoran Santic was being questioned?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me this opportunity to explain. A gentleman has already asked me how I knew that this young man's name was Zoran Santic, and I answered that I didn't learn of his identity from his ID papers, but the minutes were being taken down and I looked at the heading, and it is normal, at the top of the page, to indicate the name, and two or three sentences had been written down, and that is how I learned of the first and last name of this person. And I didn't interfere, I didn't make any suggestions; I just listened for a while and went out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We will rise now and we will reconvene at five past two sharp for re-examination. I assume, Mr. Moskowitz, you are going to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: A short re-examination. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would I like to apologise for the five minute delay -- six minute delay. I'm sorry, it's our fault. And I think we have to wait for the witness. Then while we are waiting, may I raise a matter which we would like to discuss with both parties, namely the timetable for the next week and the following weeks. We were wondering, since both the Defence counsel and the Prosecutors, as well as the Court, are busy working every day on other matters, or starting with this particular case, we thought we could have -- probably we would like to suggest a longer lunch break so that we have time to have some sort of lunch and also to work a little bit, and maybe a longer afternoon. So the idea will be to start as usual at 9.30, go on until 12.30 with a break of 30 minutes, and then in the afternoon to start again at 2.30, so after a two-hour -- lunch break, and go on without any break until 4.15. Now, the interpreters are not against it, I checked with the head of the interpreter unit, and they would agree. This would, of course, mean that we will have almost two hours, so 1 hour and 45 minutes without any break in the afternoon. So I hope the accused will not mind if we have no break. However, that would also mean that we would have a lot of time after the hearing in the afternoon to do some work. We have three other cases to deal with, and I'm sure that both the Prosecution and the Defence would probably like to have more time to prepare. Would you agree? We can't start this week, because as you know, another Chamber is sitting on another case, and they start at 9.00, and this would create practical problems if we were to start a bit earlier. No, I'm sorry, I'm wrong. No. I'm sorry. No, I'm wrong. We can start right away, namely tomorrow. What do you think? Actually, if the parties agree, we would start even tomorrow with this new schedule, and then -- now, tomorrow is the 26th, until Friday. The Friday afternoon will be off as usual. Then, as you know, on Monday, the 31st, the afternoon is off. Then the other change which I would like to announce is that on Friday, the 4th of September, we would also hold a hearing in the afternoon, because then we would not hold any hearing on the Monday, the 7th of September, and Tuesday the 8th of September. So there will be two days off, Monday and Tuesday, 7th and 8th of September. So that's why we are suggesting that we should also sit on Friday afternoon, the 4th of September, so that we don't waste too much time. Will that suit you? We apologise for this, but we have to take account of various practical problems. And as I say, with your agreement, as from tomorrow we could start with the new schedule, longer lunch break and we would stop at 4.15. I see that you agree. Yes? All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: A question, Your Honour. We would like to know the following: Until when do you expect this trial to go on? That is, will it go on for three weeks, for four weeks or maybe something else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I forgot to tell you. So far we have scheduled only proceedings for three weeks, namely will the 4th of September -- actually, four weeks, 11th of September, so for the Prosecution case; however, with the two days off, 7th and 8th of September. Now, for the following week we don't know yet, because we may have to sit on a different case, this Trial Chamber may have to sit on a different case, and we will only know on Friday, this coming Friday. But in principle, the week of the 14th of September should be off either because we sit on the other case or for other reasons. Then we would resume the following week, the 21st of September. We expect, but it is for the Prosecutor to tell us, but we expect that the Prosecution case will probably take six weeks, judging from the pace of our proceedings. We need probably six weeks -- full weeks or semi-full weeks. And then it will be for the Defence to know whether we'll have a break of one or two weeks so you can prepare, and then we would like to resume and go on, and possibly finish by the end of October or early November. Better the end of October. We are anxious to proceed as quickly as possible. Yes, Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we have this break between the end of the Prosecutors' case and the beginning of our part, we would request you to give us at least four weeks or three weeks, which was the case in the Tadic case, where they only have one accused. So we would really appreciate this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. I think three weeks probably. I mean, we are quite prepared to give you four weeks. It's just because we are concerned that the trial should be as expeditious as possible, but probably if you could do with three weeks, this could be sufficient. And, of course, that's why we also are hoping that the Prosecutor may, in a way, compress his case within probably five weeks, so that we can have then three weeks off and then we can start with the Defence case. Anyway, let us see. I see that we all share the same interest in moving on as quickly as possible. Yes. You may bring in the witness. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume after this witness, the Prosecutor will call, I assume this afternoon, Witness C. Good afternoon. Mr. Moskowitz

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would like to first attempt to clarify a misunderstanding, and just for reference to the Court and the attorneys, I believe at page 780, line 23 and 24, there was a discussion about Vlatko Kupreskic in front of the Hotel Vitez. The question that I had thought I'd asked you was how far was Mr. Kupreskic from the front door of the Hotel Vitez. The answer, I believe, that we received was 30 metres or so, and then after session one, one of the interpreters came to me and said that that had been a mistranslation of my question. The actual translation was: "How far were you," the witness, "from Vlatko Kupreskic?" The answer was 30 metres. So I would like to pose the question again to the witness. Referring now to April 15, 1993, when you testified that you saw Vlatko Kupreskic in front of the Hotel Vitez, could you tell us, from your point of view, that day how far was Mr. Kupreskic in relation to the front of the hotel, or how close was he to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Ten metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And in that regard, I think you were asked how he was dressed. You said civilian clothing. Did you notice whether Mr. Kupreskic had any kind of walking cane or any kind of medical assistance while you viewed him in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You indicated that you've seen Mr. Kupreskic in and around or in and near the hotel on more than one occasion, on several occasions. Had you ever seen Mr. Kupreskic, at that time, either in a wheelchair, or using the assistance of a cane, or having any other kind of indication that he was in medical distress?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I know Vlatko Kupreskic from our childhood, and I am making these statements not only on the basis of seeing him in front of the hotel. He never had any aides of this sort, either the wheelchair or anything similar. He was walking as formally as myself. We would pay soccer, football together, we went to school together , and I really do not know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I want to bring up another point that was brought up on cross-examination regarding the 1992 attack. Just to be perfectly clear about that, you were not in Ahmici in 1992, October, when that conflict took place, right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So you have no first-hand knowledge as to how long it may have taken the HVO forces to overtake the barrier in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You were in Vitez during that time, at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And when you were talking about four days, you were not referring to how long it took the HVO to overtake the barrier, you were referring to how long you and others were trapped at the headquarters during that period of time in Vitez. Was that what you were trying to say in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after the 1992 attack, however, you did testify that you went to Ahmici. Did you observe whether there was any damage to the minaret of the mosque after the October incident in Ahmici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to establish this when we went there with an ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You testified about that as a military person, trained military person, given the fact that the barricade was placed near the cemetery on the main road in Ahmici, could you see any legitimate military purpose for targeting the mosque's minaret?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And given the fact that the barricade was near the cemetery, could you see any legitimate military purpose for firing at the house of Mehmed Ahmic from the home across the street owned by Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You were also asked about how you knew that Vlado Santic was a commander of the military police, and you mentioned, I believe, a white belt and so forth. Let me ask you this: In your experience either as a military man and certainly as a person who was in Vitez at that time, would it have been normal for a run-of-the-mill military police officer to have an office the Hotel Vitez, the headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you spoke on frequent occasions to Vlado Santic -- let me rephrase that question. Who referred you to Vlado Santic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Usually I would contact anybody down at the hotel. Usually it was Pero Skopljak, Cerkez Marijan. For a while, that is for a lengthy period of time, there was Bertovic Anto. Basically they would, for the first time, go to see Vlado Santic and to try to take care of your problems there, and I would then establish the contact with Santic. When that was for the first time, it's very difficult for me to recall, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So it was your assumption that because you were referred to this man, that he had some authority? And by "this man" I mean Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That's how they have told me. And Cerkez was one of the commanders in the headquarters of the HVO, and Pero Skopljak. These were the people who were in charge and who told me to contact Vlado Santic who was in charge of the military police and try to take care of this. However, there were, as always, a problem. You would call up somebody and you would be told, "Well, this case was referred to somebody else." And then I was supposed to contact Blaskic. But of course, that was beyond my level, so the corps had to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You were also asked about the interview with Zoran Santic, or a young man who you recall as being identified as Zoran Santic, and there was some reference to a report being done while the interview was taking place. Now, do you know where this report was filed after the interview was completed? Or maybe not filed, but kept?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I will answer this question, but with your permission I would like to go back to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead. Answer the previous question and then we'll go to this one.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There was no problem as to who was the commander of a specific unit or what was the responsibility of the HVO in Vitez. Furthermore, in the Vitez hotel an office could be held only by those who were commanders, who held posts of commands, while the military police and the troops were stationed across the hotel in a building which in the former Yugoslavia used to be a cultural and art performing society's house. As far as this question is concerned, the minutes were kept. I mentioned before that I left Stari Vitez. There were people who stayed there who took the minutes, and the minutes were kept somewhere in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of where in Stari Vitez these minutes were kept, if you know? Or if you don't know, can you give us your best speculation on where they might be?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: While I was in Stari Vitez, they were filed in the fire brigade centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, the fire brigade centre, do you know what happened to the fire brigade centre during the siege of Stari Vitez in '92/'93 -- excuse me, the siege of Vitez in '93?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was shelled on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked questions about the civilian population in the Lasva Valley. Specifically, the question went along these lines: If you were suspicious that an attack was about to take place, why didn't you and others do something to protect the population? And I believe you provided an answer that you never suspected that really such an attack would actually take place. My question goes then -- has a slightly different thrust to it. My question is not why didn't you protect the civilian population, my question is: Could you have protected the civilian population? Could you have done so militarily?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We didn't have the arms and the weapons that would allow us to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: But you talked about, on cross-examination, having certain brigades or platoons out of Kruscica, and I believe another village was mentioned. Why couldn't you have used those brigades to provide military protection for the civilian population of Ahmici and the other villages in the valley?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. I answered to you that there was a brigade consisting only of people with no weapons, no equipment whatsoever. Part of them, a battalion, was stationed in Kruscica, and the other part was stationed in Preocica. In fact, these were just collection sites where people would gather and would then be sent to the line to fight the Serbs, Turbe, Rasic, and in Visoko, which means that all Bosniak sites, towns or towns where the majority of Bosniak ethnicity had no capabilities, could not resist, could not defend themselves. Furthermore, taking into account the fact that for hundreds of years we all lived together that until that time we never fought each other, the Croats, the Muslims, the fact that we had a common enemy, that the Croats would never attack Bosniaks, particularly that they will not attack the civilian population. And they knew very well, indeed, when we would send people to the line to fight the Serbs, because we had to make a forward announcement to be able to get our people through their checkpoints, and to get them through when they would come back from the frontlines. They would check whether weapons are being brought back from the frontlines too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You were also asked about whether you were taught, in military academy, that a surprise attack was not improper. Were you taught anything about an organised attack on a civilian population for the purpose of driving out that population from their homes, simply because of their religious beliefs? Were you taught whether that kind of attack was proper or improper?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Whether we were taught at the military academy to fight the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Never, no. At the academy, we were taught the customs and rules of war, when a soldier is fighting a soldier. And, of course, we were taught how to treat the civilians and how to treat the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Along those same lines, I believe you were asked questions about the proper military procedure for house-to-house combat, and I believe you were asked about the use of weapons and grenades and bombs, the use of those weapons in house-to-house combat. But you weren't asked whether it was normal in such combat, house-to-house combat, for soldiers to carry into such battle cans of petrol. Would that have been a common practice in house-to-house combat training that you received as training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would it have been common accepted military practice in the JNA to enter a village and conduct an operation in which virtually every single home owned by a group of persons affiliated with a religious faith, to burn every single one of their homes in a village? Would that have been common accepted military practice in house-to-house combat?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just to be perfectly clear about this, on April 16th, 1993, where was the BiH army? Were they in the Lasva Valley or were they doing other things elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: What is quite certain is that they were not in the Lasva River Valley. They were in the part of the valley around Turbe, Travnik, Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what were they busy doing that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That is where the frontlines were against the Chetniks, and we had a zone, an area, a designated area that we held because it was already said earlier on that there were no Serbs in Vitez. We didn't have a war against Serbs in Vitez. Therefore, following orders, we had to provide personnel to go elsewhere away from Vitez, that is, to the places where the frontlines were against the Serbs, and they held an area facing the Chetniks, the Serbs, at Turbe, another zone on Mount Vlasic, and another zone in Visoko, between Visoko and Breza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And did the HVO know that that's where the army was on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, they too had a squad in a part of this front but way behind our own forces, just above Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs that you know of in Ahmici for the HVO to be attacking?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, no, there were no Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I had a question which has been, to some extent, put by the Prosecutor. It is about the official records of the interrogation of Zoran Santic. So, therefore, my question is now addressed to the Prosecutor: Have you tried to get hold of those official records? Do you think there is any hope of finding those records?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have tried, and we hear that, because of the conflict in Vitez area, which I believe actually lasted longer than a year and because of the destruction in that area, it is likely that it will be impossible to recover some of these files. However, we have asked the Bosnian embassy to conduct a careful search to see if perhaps some of those files may have been saved and placed either in Sarajevo or in some other safe place. So we are waiting on a response on that, but we were given little hope that they would, in fact, be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, to explain to the Defence counsel why I put this question, is because of Rule 98 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, whereby a Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence. Of course, since we are aware that the Prosecutor has already tried to find those documents, we will not issue such an order. I think there is no objection to the witness being released, so therefore, let me thank Witness B for coming here to court to testify. You may now be released. I assume that the Prosecutor is going to call the next witness, Witness number 2, which is Witness C. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, indeed, the next witness is Witness C. The protection measures for the protection of his identity and his face have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, but the Defence has a principled objection to make. Yesterday, on the 24th, the Defence was informed that this witness would appear today, that is Witness C. May I remind those present that according to the ruling of this Trial Chamber, the Defence is entitled to be informed at least 48 hours in advance of the name of the witness who will be called to testify. It is the submission of the Defence that by calling this witness, the Prosecutor is intentionally putting the Defence in a position not to be able to prepare for the cross-examination. Also, we feel that that is in violation of the ruling of this Trial Chamber. However, on this occasion, the Defence will not cause any difficulties and agrees to the witness being heard. But we do request that should this testimony be completed ahead of time and the Defence is called to cross-examine, that that cross-examination be postponed until tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavkovic, for being so understanding. However, I must say, I myself read the witness statement on Saturday, last Saturday, so I think we all had ample opportunity to go through it. You are right, however, that we decided that you should have 48 hours to prepare for the cross-examination. I hope that, in future, the Prosecutor will give us, every Friday morning, the list of those witnesses who will be called by the Prosecutor the following week, so that they have 48 hours, the Defence has 48 hours. I think we must comply with this request. Let us proceed with this one, and again, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just comment on what has been said? The name of this witness figured on the list of witnesses disclosed to the Defence last week, at the same time as required by the Trial Chamber. Of course, we agreed to this procedure as suggested by the Trial Chamber but on condition that certain changes may occur. A change has occurred, not regarding the name of the witness but simply the order in which he will testify, and we wanted the witness to appear today before the Trial Chamber so as to shorten his stay here and to be able to return home as quickly as possible. So we have modified only the order of appearance but not the name of the witness, and the Defence has been informed as of last week regarding the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but the rule still stands regarding 48 hours, and this list was distributed on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But he was on the list since last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Defence is entitled to have 48 hours. So in principle, this witness should be asked to appear tomorrow morning. I think that we must have understanding for the position of the Defence and thank Mr. Pavkovic for agreeing to the testimony of this witness today, which means we can proceed now. It is a protected witness. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: p.m. to be reconvened on the 26th day of August, 1998 at 9.30 a.m.
